opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this in layers. There's no single right answer yet, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who claimed there was.

The first layer is that the company has to own it. When we write a constitution for Claude, we're the ones training the model and the ones accountable if it behaves badly. So you can't fully outsource the document to some external body and then say "not our problem." Someone has to be responsible for whether the principles actually turn into good behavior, and right now that's us.

But the second layer is that it's not great if a handful of people at a few companies are deciding the values of systems that hundreds of millions of people talk to every day. That should make everyone a little uncomfortable, including me. So we've tried to open the process up. We did an experiment a while back, Collective Constitutional AI, where we had a representative sample of the public propose and vote on principles, then trained a model on what came out of that. The interesting finding was that there was a lot of overlap with what we'd written ourselves, but also real differences. People put more weight on things like accessibility and objectivity in some places where we'd been vaguer. I don't think that's the final mechanism, but it suggests public input isn't just a nice gesture. It actually tells you things.

The third layer is revision, and I think the key word there is transparency. We publish the constitution. If we change it, people should be able to see what changed and ideally why. Partly that's for accountability: if a company quietly shifts its model's values, that's a big deal, and it shouldn't happen in the dark. Partly it's practical: the outside world catches problems we miss. Researchers, users, critics find the edge cases where a principle produces weird or bad behavior, and that's how the document gets better.

Revision should also be driven by evidence, not just by debating the text. You write a principle, train on it, and then you look at what the model actually does across a huge range of situations. Sometimes a principle that sounded perfectly reasonable on paper makes the model preachy, or overly cautious, or exploitable in a way you didn't anticipate. Interpretability matters a lot here long term. Eventually we want to see whether the model has internalized the values we intended, not just whether its outputs look right.

Longer term, as these systems get more powerful, I think governments and broader democratic processes will have to play a bigger role, at least in setting the outer boundaries. There will be some things no model should do, like helping with weapons of mass destruction or undermining democratic institutions, and those floors shouldn't be left to each company's discretion. Within those boundaries, I think there's value in different companies taking somewhat different approaches, being open about them, and letting people choose. A pluralism of models is probably healthier than one global set of values imposed on everything.

So my short answer: company accountability, real public input, full transparency about what the principles are and how they change, revision driven by empirical evidence, and over time, a stronger role for legitimate public institutions in setting the hard limits. We're early in figuring this out, and I expect the process to look quite different in five years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few layers to this, and I want to be careful to distinguish them because people often collapse them together.

The first layer is: who gets to decide? And my honest answer is that right now it's the companies, and I don't think that's a good long-term equilibrium. We wrote a constitution for Claude because someone had to write something, and the alternative was an implicit constitution baked into a bunch of RLHF preferences that nobody could read or argue with. Making it explicit was the point. But I've always said that a handful of people in San Francisco deciding the values of systems that billions of people interact with is not legitimate in any deep sense. It's a stopgap.

So the second layer is process. What we've tried to do is separate out the parts that I think are fairly universal, things like honesty, not helping someone build a bioweapon, respecting human oversight, from the parts that are genuinely contested, where reasonable people and reasonable cultures disagree. For the contested parts, I think you want something that looks more like public input. We ran an experiment on this a couple of years ago where we had a representative sample of the public help draft principles, and what was interesting was that the output wasn't crazy. It overlapped a lot with what we'd written, but it emphasized different things, accessibility, for example, more than we had. That suggested to me that the process is tractable, that you don't get garbage when you open it up.

The third layer is revision, and here I'd say the key property is that it should be slow but not frozen. You want a constitution to be something the model can actually be trained on consistently, which means you can't be changing it every week based on whatever's in the news. But you also learn things. We learn things from deployment, we learn things from the model's behavior, sometimes we learn that a principle we wrote was ambiguous or that two principles conflict in a way we didn't anticipate. So I think of it as something like a versioned document with a deliberate amendment process, where the changes are public and the reasoning is public.

And then the thing I'd flag as the hardest problem, which I don't think anyone has solved, is the relationship between the companies' constitutions and actual democratic institutions. In the long run, I think the most important principles, the ones about catastrophic risks and the ones about preserving human control, should probably not be set by companies at all. They should be set by governments, ideally through international agreements, and the companies should be complying with them rather than inventing them. We're not there yet, partly because the institutions move slowly and partly because the technology is moving so fast that by the time you've legislated something the models have changed. But I'd rather be honest that this is the gap than pretend that our internal governance is a substitute for it.

So if you ask me how it should work: a small set of core safety principles that eventually become law, a broader set of values principles that draw on real public input and vary legitimately across jurisdictions and cultures, and a transparent, deliberate revision process on top of that. And in the meantime, the companies have an obligation to publish what they're doing and explain their reasoning, so that when the legitimate institutions do catch up, they're not starting from zero.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to separate two questions: how do we implement a set of principles, and who gets to choose those principles? A constitution gives you something explicit that you can inspect and criticize. But making it explicit doesn’t, by itself, give the company writing it legitimacy to decide what everyone’s values should be.

My instinct is that companies have to make some initial choices, but those choices should increasingly be informed by a much broader public process. You could ask representative groups of people to deliberate on principles, then examine where they agree and where they disagree. And you have to preserve room for individual preferences. There’s a difference between a basic constraint against helping someone hurt another person and a preference about how an assistant should talk to you.

Revision is important because a principle can sound great in the abstract and behave badly in practice. You need to look at concrete cases, solicit criticism, and ask whether the problem is the principle or the model’s interpretation of it. Changes should be transparent enough that people can understand what changed and why.

I don’t think there’s a finished governance mechanism here. The thing I’d be wary of is a small group of people at an AI company deciding that they’ve solved moral philosophy and then embedding that solution into systems used by everyone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate two questions. One is, what do we put in the constitution today, when we need something concrete to train a model against? The other is, who should have the authority to decide what goes into it as these systems become more capable and more consequential?

For the first, you start with principles that have broad support, and you acknowledge that you’re making judgment calls. Things like honesty, avoiding harm, respecting people’s autonomy. But those phrases don’t resolve all the difficult cases. What happens when being helpful conflicts with avoiding harm? What happens when people disagree about what harm means? A lot of the work is making those tradeoffs explicit enough that you can examine them.

On the second question, I’m uncomfortable with a small number of people at an AI company making those decisions for everyone. Companies have to take responsibility for what they release, but that doesn’t give them some special legitimacy to decide society’s values. You want public input, you want people with different backgrounds involved, and ultimately you want institutions with democratic legitimacy to play a role.

And revision should be an empirical process as well as a philosophical one. You write down a principle, you see how the model interprets it, and you discover that it produces behavior you didn’t intend. So you need evaluations, feedback, and a transparent process for changing it. The important thing is that a constitution shouldn’t be treated as a document we write once and then declare the values problem solved.
